Process Analysis Visuals

Explore each chart in three ways. Select Enlarge chart beneath a chart to expand that chart within the activity; select the same button again to return it to its original size. Open View chart description for a concise text equivalent of the chart. Then select Show analysis to learn how the visual supports root cause investigation. All controls are keyboard accessible.

Run Chart

View chart description

Days 1–30 stay mostly between 94% and 100%, except for a drop to about 80% near day 29. After day 30, performance is lower and more variable, including lows near 70% and 60%.

Key takeaway: The downward shift and increased variation identify time periods to investigate, but they do not establish the cause.

How to use a run chart

A run chart plots a process performance measure, such as on-time delivery rate, over time. Unlike a control chart, it focuses on patterns in the sequence of data rather than statistical control limits.

Look for: trends, shifts, cycles, and unusual time periods where performance differs from the typical pattern.

Key takeaway: These patterns can show where to investigate, but they do not identify the root cause by themselves.

Boxplot

View chart description

Baseline values cluster around 95%–98%, with an 80% outlier. Current-state values are lower and more spread out, centered in the low-to-mid 80% range, with a 60% outlier.

Key takeaway: The current state shows lower typical performance and greater variation than the baseline.

How to use a boxplot

A boxplot summarizes the distribution of process performance data and makes variation and outliers easier to see.

Look for: the median, the spread of the data, differences between groups or time periods, and unusually high or low values.

Key takeaway: Variation and outliers may warrant further root cause investigation. The boxplot shows where performance differs, not why it differs.

Pareto Chart

View chart description

Waiting on scan lane is the most frequent category with 42 occurrences (52%). Adding barcode re-entry, with 19 occurrences, brings the cumulative total to 76%. The remaining categories are address/label fix (9), carrier missed (6), and pick error (4).

Key takeaway: The first two categories are logical priorities for investigation, though frequency alone does not prove root cause.

How to use a Pareto chart

A Pareto chart ranks potential causes from most to least frequent and adds a cumulative percentage line to show how much of the total is represented as categories are combined.

In this example: Waiting on the scan lane is the largest category with 42 occurrences, accounting for 52% of the total. Combined with barcode re-entry, the first two categories account for 76%.

Key takeaway: Use a Pareto chart to prioritize which causes to investigate first. Frequency helps focus the investigation, but it does not prove root cause.
